<div id="bx-article">

  <div class="bx-pills">
    <span class="bx-pill">Development</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">JavaScript</span>
    <span class="bx-pill">Performance</span>
  </div>

  <p class="bx-lede">Type a search box fast and watch your browser tab quietly slow down. Ever wondered why? You just triggered an event handler dozens of times in one second, and one of two techniques, debounce or throttle, is almost certainly the fix your code needs right now.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">01</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="javascript-debounce-vs-throttle-what-each-one-actually-controls">JavaScript Debounce vs Throttle: What Each One Actually Controls</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A keystroke, a scroll, a window resize. Each one can fire an event handler dozens or hundreds of times a second, and most of the time your code does not need to react to every single one of them.</p>

  <p>Debounce waits for a pause. It delays running your function until the events stop coming for a set amount of time, then runs it once. Throttle takes the opposite approach. It lets your function run right away, then blocks any further calls until a fixed amount of time has passed, guaranteeing a steady drip instead of a single delayed burst.</p>

  <p>That single distinction, wait for silence versus run on a schedule, is the entire javascript debounce vs throttle decision. Everything else in this guide is just showing that difference in real, running code.</p>

  <p>Chrome DevTools makes the underlying problem easy to see for yourself. Open the <a href="https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/performance/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Performance panel</a>, record a fast typing session or a scroll on an unoptimized page, and the flame chart fills with dozens of tiny, overlapping tasks that a debounce or throttle wrapper would collapse into a handful.</p>

  <p>Once you have watched both techniques fire in real code, the javascript debounce vs throttle distinction stops being two vocabulary words and starts being an actual design decision you make on purpose, handler by handler.</p>


  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">02</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="building-a-real-debounce-function-from-scratch">Building a Real debounce() Function From Scratch</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A debounce function is smaller than most people expect. It wraps your original function, and every new call cancels whatever timer was already waiting, then starts a fresh one.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">debounce.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">debounce</span>(<span class="tok-val">fn</span>, <span class="tok-val">delay</span>) {
  <span class="tok-kw">let</span> <span class="tok-val">timer</span> = <span class="tok-kw">null</span>;
  <span class="tok-kw">return function</span> (...<span class="tok-val">args</span>) {
    clearTimeout(<span class="tok-val">timer</span>);
    <span class="tok-val">timer</span> = setTimeout(() =&gt; <span class="tok-val">fn</span>.apply(<span class="tok-kw">this</span>, <span class="tok-val">args</span>), <span class="tok-val">delay</span>);
  };
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Only one thing ever happens on every call: the old timer gets thrown away and a new one takes its place. As long as new calls keep arriving before that timer finishes, the wrapped function never actually runs.</p>

  <div class="bx-tip">
    <span class="bx-tip-label">Tip</span>
    <p>Use <code>fn.apply(this, args)</code> rather than calling <code>fn()</code> directly. It preserves both the original <code>this</code> context and every argument the triggering event passed in, which matters the moment debounce wraps a method instead of a plain function.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">03</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="watching-debounce-actually-run-against-real-keystrokes">Watching debounce() Actually Run Against Real Keystrokes</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Reading the code above explains the theory. Running it against a simulated burst of keystrokes, five calls fired 80 milliseconds apart wrapped in a 300 millisecond debounce, shows exactly which calls survive and which ones get cancelled.</p>

  <p>This is the moment where javascript debounce vs throttle stops being a diagram and turns into five real console lines you can read from top to bottom.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">debounce_demo.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-val">const</span> <span class="tok-val">debouncedSearch</span> = debounce((<span class="tok-val">query</span>) =&gt; {
  console.log(<span class="tok-str">`FIRED search("${query}")`</span>);
}, <span class="tok-val">300</span>);

[<span class="tok-str">'r'</span>, <span class="tok-str">'re'</span>, <span class="tok-str">'rea'</span>, <span class="tok-str">'reac'</span>, <span class="tok-str">'react'</span>].forEach((<span class="tok-val">query</span>, <span class="tok-val">i</span>) =&gt; {
  setTimeout(() =&gt; debouncedSearch(<span class="tok-val">query</span>), <span class="tok-val">i</span> * <span class="tok-val">80</span>);
});</code></pre>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-shot">
    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real terminal output from running debounce_demo.js showing five keystroke calls to a debounced search function, with only the final call for react actually firing 300ms after the last keystroke" />
  </div>
  <p class="bx-shot-caption">Actual output from the debounce demo above. Five keystrokes went in, exactly one search call came out.</p>

  <div class="bx-fact">
    <span class="bx-fact-label">Did You Know</span>
    <p>The word debounce comes from electrical engineering, not software. A mechanical switch's metal contacts physically bounce for a few milliseconds before settling, producing several rapid electrical pulses from a single press, a well documented phenomenon covered in <a href="https://www.allaboutcircuits.com/textbook/digital/chpt-4/contact-bounce/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">All About Circuits' guide to contact bounce</a>. Software debounce solves the exact same shaped problem, just with events instead of electrons.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">04</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="building-a-real-throttle-function-from-scratch">Building a Real throttle() Function From Scratch</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>Throttle looks similar on the surface, a wrapper function holding some state in a closure, but the logic inside runs the opposite way around. The first call goes through immediately, and a cooldown flag blocks every call that follows until the limit expires.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">throttle.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-kw">function</span> <span class="tok-fn">throttle</span>(<span class="tok-val">fn</span>, <span class="tok-val">limit</span>) {
  <span class="tok-kw">let</span> <span class="tok-val">inCooldown</span> = <span class="tok-kw">false</span>;
  <span class="tok-kw">return function</span> (...<span class="tok-val">args</span>) {
    <span class="tok-kw">if</span> (<span class="tok-val">inCooldown</span>) <span class="tok-kw">return</span>;
    <span class="tok-val">fn</span>.apply(<span class="tok-kw">this</span>, <span class="tok-val">args</span>);
    <span class="tok-val">inCooldown</span> = <span class="tok-kw">true</span>;
    setTimeout(() =&gt; (<span class="tok-val">inCooldown</span> = <span class="tok-kw">false</span>), <span class="tok-val">limit</span>);
  };
}</code></pre>
  </div>

  <p>Notice what is missing compared to debounce. There is no <code>clearTimeout()</code> here at all, since throttle never cancels anything. It only ever ignores calls while the cooldown flag is still set.</p>

  <p>Both wrappers rely on the same underlying mechanism to delay work, the macrotask queue described in the <a href="https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#timers" target="_blank" rel="noopener">WHATWG HTML timer specification</a>, where every <code>setTimeout()</code> callback waits its turn behind whatever else is already scheduled.</p>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">05</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="watching-throttle-actually-run-against-real-scroll-events">Watching throttle() Actually Run Against Real Scroll Events</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>The same test structure, eight simulated scroll events fired roughly every 60 milliseconds, this time wrapped in a 200 millisecond throttle, shows a completely different pattern of survivors.</p>

  <div class="bx-code-wrap">
    <div class="bx-code-title">throttle_demo.js</div>
    <pre><code><span class="tok-val">const</span> <span class="tok-val">throttledScroll</span> = throttle((<span class="tok-val">pos</span>) =&gt; {
  console.log(<span class="tok-str">`FIRED updateStickyHeader(scrollY=${pos})`</span>);
}, <span class="tok-val">200</span>);

[<span class="tok-val">40</span>, <span class="tok-val">90</span>, <span class="tok-val">150</span>, <span class="tok-val">210</span>, <span class="tok-val">260</span>, <span class="tok-val">320</span>, <span class="tok-val">400</span>, <span class="tok-val">470</span>].forEach((<span class="tok-val">pos</span>, <span class="tok-val">i</span>) =&gt; {
  setTimeout(() =&gt; throttledScroll(<span class="tok-val">pos</span>), <span class="tok-val">i</span> * <span class="tok-val">60</span>);
});</code></pre>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-shot">
    <img src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Real terminal output from running throttle_demo.js showing eight scroll events, with the throttled function actually firing only twice, roughly 200 milliseconds apart" />
  </div>
  <p class="bx-shot-caption">Actual output from the throttle demo above. Eight scroll events went in, calls came out on a steady schedule instead of all at once.</p>

  <p>The two demos side by side make the javascript debounce vs throttle behavior almost impossible to confuse again, since the real timestamps do the explaining instead of a description of what should happen. This exact pattern, wrapping a function to control its own call frequency, is common enough that <a href="https://css-tricks.com/debouncing-throttling-explained-examples/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">CSS-Tricks has a widely referenced writeup</a> comparing several variations side by side.</p>

  <div class="bx-tip">
    <span class="bx-tip-label">Tip</span>
    <p>Pick a throttle limit that matches how often a human can actually perceive an update, usually somewhere between 100 and 250 milliseconds for a scroll or resize handler. Going much lower barely improves what a user notices while still costing extra main thread time.</p>
  </div>


  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">06</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="choosing-between-debounce-and-throttle-for-a-given-handler">Choosing Between Debounce and Throttle for a Given Handler</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>The javascript debounce vs throttle choice usually falls out naturally once you ask a simple question about the handler in front of you. Does the user care about the very last state, or does the user care about a steady stream of updates the whole time an action is happening? Making the right javascript debounce vs throttle call up front avoids retrofitting the other pattern into a handler later.</p>

  <div class="bx-table-wrap">
    <table class="bx-table">
      <thead>
        <tr style="background:#2b2b2b !important;">
          <th style="background:#2b2b2b !important; color:#ffffff !important;">Event Handler</th>
          <th style="background:#2b2b2b !important; color:#ffffff !important;">Better Fit</th>
          <th style="background:#2b2b2b !important; color:#ffffff !important;">Why</th>
        </tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>Search box autocomplete</td><td>Debounce</td><td>Only the final, complete query is worth sending to an API</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Sticky header on scroll</td><td>Throttle</td><td>The header needs to keep updating the whole time the page scrolls</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Window resize layout recalculation</td><td>Debounce</td><td>Recalculating mid drag wastes work the final size will replace</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Infinite scroll load trigger</td><td>Throttle</td><td>The scroll position check needs to keep running as the user scrolls</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Form field validation</td><td>Debounce</td><td>Validating after the user pauses feels less naggy than every keystroke</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">07</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="where-this-actually-matters-for-real-site-performance">Where This Actually Matters for Real Site Performance</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>An unthrottled scroll handler is a classic way to quietly wreck a page's <a href="/interaction-to-next-paint-inp-explained/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Interaction to Next Paint score</a>, since every single scroll event competes with the browser for main thread time.</p>

  <p>The same problem shows up as inflated <a href="/what-is-total-blocking-time-tbt/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Total Blocking Time</a> during a Lighthouse audit, where long, uninterrupted JavaScript tasks push the main thread past the point where it can respond to input quickly.</p>

  <p>A feature like the scroll based heading highlighter in <a href="/auto-highlight-current-heading-scrolling/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">automatically highlighting the current heading while scrolling</a>, or the position tracking behind a <a href="/sticky-table-of-contents-css-javascript/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">sticky table of contents built with CSS and JavaScript</a>, both depend on a scroll listener that runs constantly, which makes them a textbook case for throttle rather than debounce.</p>

  <p>Google's own <a href="https://web.dev/articles/inp" target="_blank" rel="noopener">guidance on Interaction to Next Paint</a> specifically calls out unthrottled scroll and input handlers as one of the most common causes of a slow score, which lines up exactly with what the real timestamps earlier in this guide showed. Every javascript debounce vs throttle decision made in a real codebase eventually shows up in a Core Web Vitals report, for better or worse.</p>

  <div class="bx-fact">
    <span class="bx-fact-label">Did You Know</span>
    <p><a href="https://lodash.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Lodash</a>, one of the most widely used JavaScript utility libraries, ships its own <code>debounce</code> and <code>throttle</code> implementations with extra options like a leading edge call and a maximum wait time, both handled manually in the plain versions built earlier in this guide. Its <a href="https://github.com/lodash/lodash" target="_blank" rel="noopener">source on GitHub</a> is worth reading once the hand rolled version above feels familiar.</p>
  </div>


  <div class="bx-section-head">
    <span class="bx-num">08</span>
    <h2 class="bx-h2" id="common-mistakes-when-implementing-debounce-and-throttle">Common Mistakes When Implementing Debounce and Throttle</h2>
    <div class="bx-rule"></div>
  </div>

  <p>A hand rolled debounce or throttle function is short enough to get subtly wrong, and most of the javascript debounce vs throttle bugs that reach production trace back to the same handful of mistakes.</p>

  <ul class="bx-checklist">
    <li><b>Creating a new debounced function on every render:</b> in a framework like React, defining the wrapped function inside a component body resets its internal timer state constantly. Create it once, outside the render path.</li>
    <li><b>Forgetting to remove the event listener on cleanup:</b> a debounced or throttled handler still attached to a removed element keeps a timer alive and can fire against state that no longer exists.</li>
    <li><b>Using debounce where users expect immediate feedback:</b> a button that visibly does nothing for 300 milliseconds reads as broken, not careful. Throttle, or a short debounce under 100 milliseconds, usually feels better here.</li>
    <li><b>Never testing the actual timing:</b> logging real timestamps, the same way the two demos above did, catches an off by one delay value long before a user does.</li>
    <li><b>Reaching for a library before trying the plain version:</b> both functions are well under fifteen lines. Understanding the two above makes reading <a href="https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/EventTarget/addEventListener" target="_blank" rel="noopener">MDN's addEventListener reference</a> and any library's implementation far easier later.</li>
  </ul>

    <div class="bx-faq">
    <h3 class="bx-h3">Frequently Asked Questions</h3>

    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">1</span><span>What is the simplest way to explain javascript debounce vs throttle?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Debounce waits for a pause and then runs once. Throttle runs immediately and then blocks further calls for a fixed window, no matter how many more events arrive.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">2</span><span>Can debounce and throttle be used together on the same handler?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Rarely needed, but yes. A throttle can keep a handler responsive during a long event burst while a trailing debounce call handles the final, settled state once the burst ends.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">3</span><span>Does debounce delay the very first call too?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Yes, in the plain version built in this guide. A leading edge variant exists that runs the first call immediately and then debounces the rest, which Lodash's implementation supports as an option.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">4</span><span>Is throttle better than debounce for scroll events?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Usually, yes. A scroll listener that needs to keep updating the page while scrolling happens, like a sticky header or a progress bar, fits throttle's steady schedule far better than debounce's single delayed call.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">5</span><span>What delay value should a debounce or throttle actually use?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>Somewhere between 150 and 400 milliseconds covers most search inputs and form validation. Scroll and resize handlers usually work well between 100 and 250 milliseconds, though the real test is watching how the interaction actually feels.</p></div>
    </div>
    <div class="bx-faq-item">
      <button type="button" class="bx-faq-q"><span class="bx-faq-num">6</span><span>Do modern frameworks handle debounce and throttle automatically?</span></button>
      <div class="bx-faq-a"><p>No framework does this for you by default. React, Vue, and similar tools still expect the developer to wrap an event handler manually, usually with the same closure based pattern shown in this guide.</p></div>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="bx-learn">
    <h2 id="what-we-learn-today">What We Learn Today</h2>
    <div class="bx-learn-grid">
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">1</span><div><h4>Debounce waits for a pause</h4><p>It only runs once the calls actually stop.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">2</span><div><h4>Throttle runs on a schedule</h4><p>It fires immediately, then blocks calls until the limit passes.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">3</span><div><h4>Both wrap a function in a closure</h4><p>Timer or cooldown state lives inside that closure.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">4</span><div><h4>Real timing beats assumed timing</h4><p>Logging real timestamps caught the exact behavior of each.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">5</span><div><h4>Scroll and resize favor throttle</h4><p>They need updates the whole time an action happens.</p></div></div>
      <div class="bx-learn-card"><span class="bx-learn-num">6</span><div><h4>Search and validation favor debounce</h4><p>Only the final, settled value is usually worth acting on.</p></div></div>
    </div>
  </div>


  <div class="bx-cta">
    <h3>Ready to Stop Your Event Handlers From Overworking?</h3>
    <p>Debounce and throttle are two of the smallest functions in this entire guide, and among the highest impact changes you can make to a page that feels sluggish under fast user input.</p>
    <div class="bx-cta-btns">
      <a href="/core-web-vitals-2026/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Read the Core Web Vitals Guide</a>
      <a href="/how-to-improve-mobile-page-speed/" target="_blank" rel="noopener" class="bx-cta-outline">Improve Mobile Page Speed</a>
    </div>
  </div>

</div>

<script>
(function() {
  var items = document.querySelectorAll('.bx-faq-item');

  items.forEach(function(item) {
    var q = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-q');
    var a = item.querySelector('.bx-faq-a');

    item.classList.add('open');
    a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';

    q.addEventListener('click', function() {
      var isOpen = item.classList.contains('open');
      if (isOpen) {
        item.classList.remove('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = null;
      } else {
        item.classList.add('open');
        a.style.maxHeight = a.scrollHeight + 'px';
      }
    });
  });
})();
</script>
